title: When Only Whole Numbers Count
question: What changes about an equation when only whole-number answers are allowed?
hook: Half a box or a third of a coin makes no sense, and that small rule makes some equations very hard.
idea: Diophantine equations ask for whole-number solutions, and beyond the simplest cases there is no general method for deciding whether any exist.

beats.prompt: match each name to what it describes
pairs: A sum of unknowns with coefficients equals a constant
The part of algebraic geometry that studies the curves and surfaces such systems define
The study of Diophantine problems that Diophantus began
beats.explain: Each name marks a different way of looking at whole-number equations: by the shape of the equation or by the study built around it.

beats.prompt: Someone proposes writing one computer program that checks any Diophantine equation and reports whether it has a whole-number solution. What does Hilbert's tenth problem say about this plan?

choices.label: Such a general program cannot exist
It can exist but would be too slow to be practical
choices.feedback: It sounds like a speed problem, but the result is stronger: no such general method exists at all, however much time it gets.

choices.label: It exists, but only for equations with a single unknown
choices.feedback: This sounds like a sensible restriction, but the result is about arbitrary equations and says no general algorithm exists.

beats.explain: Hilbert's tenth problem shows that there cannot exist a general algorithm that decides whether an arbitrary Diophantine equation has an integer solution.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Diophantus of Alexandria studied these equations in the 3rd century.
Individual equations have been treated as puzzles throughout history.
So a general theory covering every kind of equation must have been finished soon after Diophantus.
In fact, general theories beyond linear and quadratic equations came only in the twentieth century.
beats.explain: Puzzles are old, but general theories beyond the linear and quadratic cases only arrived in the twentieth century, so the third step does not follow.

beats.prompt: Mathematicians have general methods that work on almost every cubic equation seen in practice. What can be said about all cubic equations?

choices.label: A method for every cubic equation has been proven impossible to improve
choices.feedback: This sounds like the final word, but nothing in that claim is known.

choices.label: No algorithm is known that works for every cubic equation
Cubic equations are easier to solve than quadratic ones
choices.feedback: Cubic cases feel like a small step up, but degree-two equations are the easier ones.

beats.explain: Methods cover almost all cubic equations met in practice, yet no algorithm is known for every cubic one, and degree-two equations are easier.
